--- Page 1 ---
FrontierOR Challenge White Paper 2026
Version 1.0, 20 November 2026
The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for
Operations Research
Organizers
Hai Wang, Bretislav Hajek, Chonghe Jiang, Minwei Kong,
Ao Qu, Huatian Gong, Bo Dong
Cynthia Barnhart, Jinhua Zhao
frontieror.competition@gmail.com
Abstract
Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new
routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it
is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve
code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in
the FrontierOR benchmark’s one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi,
with an objective within 1% of Gurobi’s and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances.
The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and
improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the
benchmark’s 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation
types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark,
with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the
submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in
the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software,
within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution
scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.
Keywords: Operations research, combinatorial optimization, LLM agents, automated
algorithm design, competition
1. Introduction
The FrontierOR Challenge1 asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and
improve algorithms for optimization problems, instead of hand-tuning a single algorithm.
The main scientific question is the following: “Can an LLM agent design algorithms that are
feasible, good and fast on instances it has never seen, across many optimization problems
and under a fixed compute budget?”
Optimization problems span many categories, such as routing, scheduling and network
design. For each of them, the OR literature studies specialized algorithms: decompositions,
branch-and-price, problem-specific heuristics. General-purpose solvers help, but a correct
formulation often still requires a deep understanding of the domain. Within a one-hour time
limit, Gurobi does not reach optimality on 46% of the large FrontierOR instances (Kong et al.,
2026a). LLM-driven program search has started to change this. FunSearch (Romera-Paredes
et al., 2024) and AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) found new constructions by evolving
1. https://frontieror-challenge.com
© 2026 H. Wang et al.
arXiv:2611.26171v1  [cs.AI]  19 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
Wang et al.
programs, and EoH (Liu et al., 2024) and ReEvo (Ye et al., 2024) evolve heuristics for
combinatorial problems. In optimization modeling, AlphaOPT builds and refines a library of
reusable insights based on solver feedback to guide LLMs in formulating new problems (Kong
et al., 2026b). Benchmarks measure the gap that remains: CO-Bench (Sun et al., 2026),
HeuriGym (Chen et al., 2026), ALE-Bench (Imajuku et al., 2025) and FrontierOR (Kong
et al., 2026a) all find that agents trail expert algorithms and commercial solvers, and that
consistency across problems is the weakest point. In FrontierOR’s one-shot setting, a model
writes one program per problem from its statement, with a few self-debugging rounds on
execution errors. In the latest evaluation, the strongest model, Claude Fable 5, returns a
feasible solution within 1% of or better than Gurobi’s reference objective, in no more than
Gurobi’s wall-clock time, on 39% of the large instances across all 180 problems. Results in
this competition may differ, since the Main track allows only open-source libraries, whereas
in FrontierOR the generated algorithms could call Gurobi.
The competition captures a practical scenario: a practitioner faces a new decision problem
with a written statement, a data format, and a deadline, and needs an algorithm that works
on unseen instances. Each team receives the problem definitions, builds a pipeline that turns
each one into an algorithm, and is scored on hidden instances. The competition runs in two
stages: a qualification on 60 problems from the FrontierOR benchmark, released 15 per week,
and a final on new problems, and in two tracks: the Main track, where we run the submitted
algorithms under fixed compute with open-source dependencies, and the Self-hosted track,
where teams solve the instances on their own infrastructure with any software, including
commercial solvers.
We expect the competition to contribute (1) a public comparison of agentic algorithm
design methods under one protocol, with independent checkers and hidden instances; (2) ev-
idence for practitioners on whether an agent can replace weeks of expert work on a new
problem; (3) new problems and instances for the OR community, through a call for contri-
butions; and (4) released problems, checkers and descriptions of the top teams’ methods
after the competition.
2. Related Competitions
Earlier competitions at the intersection of machine learning and OR focused on one part
of the pipeline.
NL4Opt (Ramamonjison et al., 2022) asked for formulations of small
linear programs from text. ML4CO (Gasse et al., 2022) replaced heuristic components
inside a MIP solver on three datasets. The DIMACS Implementation Challenges2 and the
ROADEF/EURO Challenge3 pose one problem per edition to human algorithm designers,
as do the AtCoder Heuristic Contests,4 which ALE-Bench (Imajuku et al., 2025) later used
to evaluate AI systems.
To our knowledge, no earlier competition combines four features: one workflow must
cover many problems at once, so that generality is rewarded over tuning for a single problem;
on the Main track, the scored submission is algorithm code that the organizers run on
hidden instances under fixed compute, rather than a formulation or a set of solutions; every
2. http://dimacs.rutgers.edu/programs/challenge/
3. https://www.roadef.org/challenge/
4. https://atcoder.jp/
2


--- Page 3 ---
FrontierOR Challenge
solution passes an independent checker that recomputes the objective; and the final stage
tests transfer to problems outside the published benchmark. The Self-hosted track scores
uploaded solutions instead.
3. Competition Format
Teams
Participants enter through the competition portal as teams of one or more people.
Each person holds only one account and belong to only one team at a time. A team chooses
the Main or Self-hosted track when it is created. Registration and team formation close
at 23:59 EST (UTC-5) on 27 December 2026. Teams may change their track before this
deadline; afterward, their track is fixed for the competition.
Stage 1: Qualification
Stage 1 runs from 00:00 EST (UTC-5) on 4 January 2027 until
23:59 EST on 31 January 2027. Sixty problems are released in four weekly rounds of 15.
The rounds open at 00:00 EST on 4, 11, 18 and 25 January, respectively, and each remains
open for exactly seven days. A submission covers only the currently open round. Main-track
submissions must be accepted by the portal before the round closes; their evaluation may
finish afterward. Self-hosted uploads must meet the applicable instance, submission-window,
and round deadlines. Teams follow a public leaderboard that accumulates results across
rounds.
Main Track: Algorithm Design
Teams submit algorithm code, the scored submission,
which we run in a sandbox with no network, 2 vCPU and 4 GB of memory. Only open-source
dependencies are allowed. The overall champion comes from this track.
Self-hosted Track: Tool-Augmented Solving
Teams solve the instances on their own
machines, by any means, including commercial solvers, and upload solutions within a timed
window. The uploaded solutions are scored; we verify the solutions, not the process.
Qualification for Stage 2
Finalists are selected separately within each track using the
final Stage 1 ranking across all 60 problems, after eligible submissions have been evaluated
and eligibility checks have been completed. Teams are ranked by score S, highest first, and
then by normalized time U, lowest first (Section 5). The number of finalist places in each
track is TBA and will be announced when Stage 1 ends. If teams remain tied on both S and
U at the qualification cutoff, all such tied teams advance, even if this increases the number
of finalists.
Stage 2: Final
Stage 2 takes place on 8–14 February 2027 and introduces new problems
outside the published benchmark, with unseen instances. Main-track finalists submit both
their algorithm code and the source code of the agentic framework used to produce it.
Self-hosted finalists submit solution files only. Final rankings are determined on a private
final dataset. Detailed Stage 2 rules will be published on 1 February 2027, when Stage 1
ends, and will specify the exact development and submission deadlines, submission formats,
and verification requirements.
Leaderboards
Each stage has one leaderboard per track; the two tracks are never
compared. Each problem category and each formulation is also ranked on its own (Section 4).
Baselines run by the organizers appear as unranked reference bands (Section 7).

--- Page 4 ---

4. Datasets
Source
The problems come from the FrontierOR benchmark (Kong et al., 2026a): 180
problems derived from methodologically diverse papers in leading OR venues. Its audited
release (FrontierOR Team, 2026) covers all 180, with 1,080 instance/reference pairs, each
reference accepted by the problem’s checker. Every problem comes with a natural-language
statement, instance and solution schemas, a feasibility checker, instances with 102 to 107
variables and constraints, and reference solutions computed with Gurobi. Each problem has
a slug named after its source paper, such as barnhart2000.
Stage 1 Problems
The organizers select 60 of the 180 problems for Stage 1, none of
them from the testing stage, chosen to cover diverse problem classes, formulations, objective
directions and algorithm runtimes. Each problem has two labels (Table 1): a category, the
application domain it comes from, and a formulation, the mathematical form of the model
behind it. A round’s problems stay hidden until the round opens.
Table 1: Problem categories and formulations. Every problem has one of each. The examples
are illustrative.
Category
Example problems
Routing
vehicle routing variants, dial-a-ride, orienteering
Production & Inventory
lot sizing, production planning
Scheduling
crew scheduling, machine scheduling
Packing & Partitioning
bin packing, cutting, set partitioning
Graph & Quadratic Optimization
graph partitioning, quadratic assignment
Network Design & Location
multicommodity flow, facility location
Formulation
Model
Combinatorial
discrete choices of routes, sequences, sets or assignments
Mixed-integer
linear models with integer and continuous variables
Quadratic
quadratic objective or constraints
Stochastic
uncertain data given by scenarios or distributions
Robust & bilevel
worst case over an uncertainty set, or a leader and a follower
Instance Sets
Each problem has three disjoint sets of instances. Public instances are
published for development and accessible to registered teams; they are never scored. Private
Main instances score the Main-track submissions and are never published. Private Self-hosted
instances score the Self-hosted track; Self-hosted teams receive them during a submission, so
they are kept apart from the Main set. Instances are generated iteratively: random instances
are generated for each problem, their difficulty is evaluated with Gurobi, and generation
continues until the set has the desired difficulty.
Reference Objectives
Each private instance has a reference objective z∗: a good checker-
accepted objective. Reference solutions are computed with long-running Gurobi solves or
specialized algorithms for the given problem.
4


--- Page 5 ---
FrontierOR Challenge
Example
Appendix A gives a complete problem from the testing stage, barnhart2000:
its statement, instance schema and solution schema.
Contributions
Anyone registered may propose a new problem, or new instances for an
existing problem. Each contribution should include a description, related work and files.
Each contribution is reviewed individually and used to extend the benchmark. Accepted
contributions are credited to the contributors.
5. Evaluation Metrics
Each solution is checked, scored by its ratio to its instance’s reference, and the instance
scores are averaged into a submission score. Only private instances count.
Feasibility
The checker verifies every constraint and recomputes the objective from the
decisions. A reported objective value that disagrees with the recomputed one beyond the
objective tolerance is rejected; otherwise, the recomputed value z is the one scored. In the
testing stage and Stage 1, each problem’s checker is published with it, as the evaluation runs
it, so teams can check feasibility themselves; Stage 2 checkers are not published. Teams see
the verdict for each instance.
Instance Score
A feasible solution with objective z is scored against the reference objective
z∗. A solution is better than the reference when z < z∗for minimization and z > z∗for
maximization. The score is
s =

2

if zz∗≤0 and z is worse than z∗.
(1)
For positive objectives, minimization scores z∗/z and maximization scores z/z∗; for negative
objectives the two ratios swap. Either way, matching the reference scores 1, a worse solution
less and a better one more, up to the cap of 2. When z and z∗have opposite signs, or either
is 0, a ratio has no meaningful scale: a better solution scores 2, an equal one 1 and a worse
one 0. An instance scores 0 when there is no feasible solution: the algorithm exceeded the
time limit or the memory limit, crashed, wrote no readable solution, or the checker rejected
it.
Tolerances
Each problem’s checker sets its own tolerances. Constraints, including integral-
ity, must hold within an absolute tolerance, typically 10−5. The reported objective value
must agree with the recomputed objective within a relative tolerance, usually 0.5%, depend-
ing on the problem. The score adds no tolerance of its own: z = z∗only when the two values
are identical, and only an objective of exactly 0 counts as zero.
Time Limits
The score rewards quality only, so speed is enforced through the time
limits instead. Each problem falls into one of three time classes, with a limit of 10 seconds,
60 seconds or 5 minutes per instance. The classification is based on problem difficulty and
application domain. The testing stage uses 60 seconds for every problem.

the private instances of problem p in the team’s track; every one of them is scored. The
submission’s problem scores and its round score are

Every problem weighs the same, however many instances it has. The denominator is always
the whole round: a partial submission scores 0 on every instance of a problem it has no
algorithm for (Self-hosted: on every instance without an uploaded solution).
Stage Score
In each round, exactly one submission counts: the team’s completed sub-
mission with the highest Rr. All the round’s problem scores come from that submission;
a round’s result is never assembled from the best problem scores of different submissions.
Among submissions with equal Rr, the one with the lower time Ur (below) counts, then the
earliest. The stage score is the mean over the problems P of all rounds opened so far,

problems stay in P. Since S grows with each Rr, the counted submissions are also those
that maximize S.
Ranking
Teams are ranked by S, highest first. Scores are compared without rounding,
and rounded to four decimal places for leaderboard display. Equal scores are ranked by the
time U, lowest first, and teams equal on both share a rank. U is averaged like S, over the
same instances and problems, from the time each instance used as a share of the most it
could use:

and Ur is the mean of Up over Pr. Here ti is the algorithm’s wall time on the Main track
and the time from download to upload on the Self-hosted track, and Tp is the problem’s
time limit, plus the 60-second upload grace on the Self-hosted track. An instance without a
feasible solution counts the full time whatever the reason: a time-out, a crash, an infeasible
or rejected solution, a skipped instance, a problem without an algorithm or a missing upload.
Every problem of a round without a submission has Up = 1. Leaving work undone therefore
never lowers U, and a fast failure ties with a slow one. A category or a formulation is ranked
the same way, by the mean of Sp and then of Up over its released problems.

Discussion
The ratio is simple to explain and normalizes each instance by its own reference,
so problems with objectives of very different magnitude can be averaged. It has known
limits, which we accept for the first edition: it is not invariant to a constant offset in the
objective, so a problem whose objective is mostly a fixed cost compresses all teams near 1
and weighs less in the ranking than its equal weight suggests; and weak references inflate
scores up to the cap.
6. Evaluation Protocol
Algorithm Contract
A Main-track submission is a zip or tar.gz archive of up to 4 MB
with one folder per problem, named by its slug, each holding a solve.py. Each folder is
mounted on its own, so algorithms cannot share code. The sandbox runs
python solve.py --problem <slug> --instance /work/in/instance.json \
--output /work/out/solution.json --time-limit <seconds>
and expects a JSON object with a numeric objective value and the decisions the problem’s
solution schema defines. Algorithms are Python only; teams who want another language use
the Self-hosted track.
Environment
Our images run Python 3.12 or 3.14 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, NetworkX,
OR-Tools, PuLP, HiGHS and Pyomo, and their full lockfiles are published. A team may add
up to 50 open-source packages from PyPI, within the documented installation and resource
limits; they are installed once before the first run, outside the time limit, and reused by later
submissions with the same list.
Main-Track Execution
Each instance runs in its own gVisor5 sandbox with no network,
2 vCPU, 4 GB of memory, 1 GB of disk, a read-only algorithm folder and the problem’s
time limit (Figure 1). Each problem’s public instances run first; if the algorithm fails on
one, the problem’s private instances are skipped and score 0. The checker then verifies each
solution. Teams see each instance’s score or the reason it scored 0, but no algorithm logs,
objective values or run times for private instances, since these could reveal the instances.
Self-hosted Submissions
Opening a submission starts a time window long enough to
solve every private instance of the round one after another, each within its time limit plus
the grace below, plus 15 minutes. The team starts each private instance separately. The
instance submission process consists of: starting the evaluation window, downloading the
instance data, solving the instance locally, and uploading the solution. Each instance has its
time limit (the same as on the Main track) plus 60 seconds of grace for the download and
upload. Uploads are final. The submission closes when the last solution is uploaded, after
which the checker and scoring run on our server, with the same scoring as the Main track.
Infrastructure
The portal and API run as a web application backed by PostgreSQL
and object storage. Submissions are queued and evaluated by an autoscaling fleet of CPU
workers on AWS, each job receiving a whole worker’s 2 vCPU and 4 GB. Failures on our
side are retried; an instance that still fails after three tries scores 0. Each team has one
submission per UTC day, four during the testing stage.

one job per instance and runs each in its own gVisor sandbox, and the scores

same path once its window closes, with only the checker running on the uploaded
solutions.
7. Baselines and Starter Code
Starter Repository
A public starter repository6 works for both tracks. Its example agent
receives a problem and must produce a function solve(instance, time limit s): it asks
a model for code, tests it on the public instances, and asks for fixes until it works. The
prompt adapts FrontierOR’s one-shot prompt to the challenge: open-source solvers instead of
Gurobi, 2 CPUs, and a function instead of a whole program. A toolkit simplifies the process
of downloading the problems, running the agent on every problem, testing the algorithms on
the public instances (optionally in the sandbox’s Docker image), and submitting the results.
Competitors should further extend this starter code to build their own agentic workflows.
Baselines
The organizers run the starter code with several frontier models and submit
the results through the same API and sandbox as any team. This results in the baseline
solutions shown on the leaderboard. Baseline scores appear on the Stage 1 leaderboard as
each round opens; a later version of this paper reports them.
8. Rules
Eligibility
Participants must hold only one account and belong to one team.
Dependencies
On the Main track, commercial solvers and remote services are not available
in the sandbox, and extra packages must be open source. Packages are not all checked
automatically; prize-eligible submissions may be audited. The Self-hosted track permits any
software.
6. https://github.com/Alpha-Z-Pte-Ltd/frontieror-challenge-starter
8


--- Page 9 ---
FrontierOR Challenge
Fair Play
Algorithms code must not try to escape the sandbox, access the network, tamper
with the evaluation or read instances it was not given. Private instances are confidential:
they must not be extracted, reconstructed or shared, and Self-hosted teams must not pass
their instances to anyone. Collusion between teams and the use of several accounts or teams
to gain submissions are prohibited. The organizers decide questions of scoring, eligibility
and interpretation, and may disqualify a submission or team that breaks the rules.
Intellectual Property
Teams keep ownership of their code and solutions. They grant the
organizers a non-exclusive, royalty-free license to store, execute, evaluate and analyze them
in order to run and verify the competition, and to publish scores and rankings. Submitted
code and solutions are not published without the team’s permission; winning approaches
may be described in aggregate or with consent.
Ethics and Accessibility
The problems come from published literature and contain no
personal data. Participation is free. On the Main track the organizers provide the evaluation
compute, so a team needs only a laptop and access to an LLM for its agent. The cost of
LLM calls falls on the teams, which can favor well-funded groups.
9. Timeline and Awards
Timeline
Table 2 gives the schedule. The initial registration and testing stage is intended
to let teams familiarize themselves with the portal and the submission process. This stage is
also intended to let the organizers test the infrastructure and the scoring. Stage 1 releases the
60 competition problems used for qualification scoring in four weekly rounds of 15 problems.

Awards
Table 3 lists the awards. The prizes go to the overall ranking, which comes from
the Main track, for a pool of US$21,000. Recognitions reward results and contributions
beyond the ranking: the winner of each sub-track, that is each problem category and each
formulation (Section 4), the best new problem or instance suite, and the best write-up of an
agent’s methodology, architecture and findings. Sub-track winners are announced with the
results.

10. Organisation
The challenge is organized by FrontierOR, MIT and Alpha Z. The FrontierOR team (Kong
et al., 2026a) provides the benchmark, its audit and the checkers; Alpha Z builds and
runs the portal and the evaluation infrastructure. The executive committee is Hai Wang
(chair), Chonghe Jiang, Minwei Kong, Ao Qu, Bretislav Hajek and Huatian Gong. The
advisory committee is Cynthia Barnhart and Jinhua Zhao from MIT. The organizers provide
the portal, the problems, instances and checkers, the starter repository and baselines, and
support by email. Alpha Z sponsors the prize pool and the evaluation compute.
11. Conclusion
The goal of this competition is to find out whether agentic workflows can design OR
algorithms that hold up on unseen data, across many problems and under a fixed budget.
To that end, we propose 60 of the 180 audited FrontierOR problems in a qualification stage
of weekly rounds, three time classes, new problems in a final stage, independent checkers,
hidden instances and two tracks that separate algorithm design under fixed compute from
tool-augmented solving.
Acknowledgments
We thank the authors of the FrontierOR benchmark for the data and checkers, and Alpha Z
for sponsoring the prize pool and the evaluation compute.

Appendix A. Example Problem
The testing stage’s barnhart2000, Origin-Destination Integer Multicommodity Flow, comes
from Barnhart et al. (2000). Below are its statement and schemas as published on the
problem page. The schemas are annotated examples: each value gives its type in angle
brackets, then its meaning, and a list shows one element. The objective is minimized.
Statement
A telecommunications network operator manages a directed network consisting
of a set of nodes and a set of directed arcs connecting pairs of nodes. Each arc has a known
capacity, expressed in units of bandwidth. The operator must handle a set of commodities,
where each commodity represents a group of calls or messages sharing a common origin
node and a common destination node. Each commodity has a known demand quantity
representing the bandwidth it requires.
Every commodity must be routed as a single, unsplittable unit along exactly one directed
path from its origin node to its destination node, or it may be rejected entirely.
To
allow rejection, the network includes, for each commodity, an artificial direct arc from
the commodity’s origin to its destination. The artificial arc has no capacity limit and
carries a cost equal to the revenue that would have been earned by successfully routing that
commodity. All physical arcs in the network have zero routing cost for every commodity.
The operator must choose, for each commodity, exactly one origin-to-destination path
(which may be the artificial rejection arc or any path through the physical network). The
total demand flowing through any physical arc, summed across all commodities whose chosen
paths include that arc, must not exceed the arc’s capacity. Flow must be conserved at every
node for every commodity: at the origin node of a commodity, exactly one unit of that
commodity’s flow is produced; at the destination node, exactly one unit is absorbed; and
at every intermediate node, the total flow of that commodity entering the node equals the
total flow leaving it.
The goal is to minimize the total cost. For each combination of commodity and arc,
the cost contribution equals the commodity’s demand multiplied by the per-unit cost for
that commodity on that arc, counted only when that arc lies on the commodity’s chosen
path. The total cost is the sum of these contributions across all commodities and all arcs.
Because physical arcs have zero cost, the total cost reduces to the sum of artificial-arc
costs for rejected commodities, which equals the total lost revenue from commodities not
routed through the physical network. Equivalently, minimizing total cost maximizes the
total revenue earned from commodities successfully carried on the physical network.
Instance Schema
{
"network": {
"num_nodes": "<int> Total number of nodes in the directed network.",
"num_arcs": "<int> Total number of directed physical arcs in the network.",
"nodes": "<list[int], length num_nodes> Identifiers for all nodes in the network.",
"arcs": [
{
"arc_id": "<int> Unique identifier for this arc.",
"from_node": "<int> Node where this directed arc originates.",
"to_node": "<int> Node where this directed arc terminates.",
"capacity": "<int> Maximum total bandwidth that can flow through this arc across
all commodities.",

FrontierOR Challenge
"cost": "<int> Per-unit routing cost for any commodity using this arc."
}
]
},
"commodities": {
"num_commodities": "<int> Total number of commodities (call groups) to be routed or
rejected.",
"commodity_list": [
{
"commodity_id": "<int> Unique identifier for this commodity.",
"origin": "<int> Node where this commodity originates.",
"destination": "<int> Node where this commodity must be delivered.",
"demand": "<int> Bandwidth required by this commodity.",
"revenue": "<int> Revenue earned if this commodity is successfully routed through
the physical network.",
"artificial_arc_cost": "<int> Cost incurred if this commodity is rejected instead
of being routed."
}
]
},
"objective": "<str> Direction of optimization for the total routing and rejection cost."
}
Solution Schema
{
"objective_value": "<float> Total cost of rejected commodities across the entire routing
plan.",
"commodities": [
{
"commodity_id": "<int> Identifier of the commodity whose routing outcome is described
in this entry.",
"rejected": "<bool> Whether this commodity is rejected and sent on its artificial arc
instead of being routed through the network.",
"path_arcs": [
{
"from": "<int> Origin node of an arc used on this commodity's routing path.",
"to": "<int> Destination node of an arc used on this commodity's routing path.",
"arc_id": "<int> Identifier of an arc used on this commodity's routing path."
}
]
}
]
}
On the public tiny instance, an example algorithm finds a feasible solution with objective
111 against a reference of 64, which would score 64/111 ≈0.5766.
